title: HDI 2025: South Africa, a Giant with Feet of Clay
excerpt: South Africa remains one of the continent's most developed countries, but its Human Development Index shows sharp contrasts between economic gains, inequality and social challenges.
seo_title: HDI 2025: South Africa, a Giant with Feet of Clay
seo_desc: South Africa's 2025 HDI of 0.713 keeps it among Africa's leaders, but inequality, unemployment and poverty continue to hold back progress.
image_alt: Skyline of Johannesburg, South Africa, as its 2025 Human Development Index is assessed
body_html:
Johannesburg, 19 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – South Africa remains one of the most developed countries on the African continent, but its Human Development Index (HDI) reveals a more contrasting reality than it appears. Between economic progress, persistent inequality and social challenges, the Rainbow Nation is still trying to reconcile growth and fairness.

An HDI edging up, but still unequal

According to the latest report of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), South Africa posts an HDI of 0.713 in 2025, placing the country in the "high human development" category. This figure keeps it at the top of the sub-Saharan Africa rankings, alongside Mauritius (0.805) and Seychelles (0.798).

This performance rests on modern infrastructure, a diversified economy (mining, the automotive industry, finance, tourism) and relatively broad access to education and healthcare. However, behind this facade of progress, the gaps between social classes and regions remain wide.

Social divides hold back progress

Despite public policies focused on reducing inequality, nearly 18 million South Africans still live below the poverty line, according to World Bank estimates. Unemployment, which affects around 31% of the active population, remains one of the highest on the continent.

Rural areas, particularly in Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal provinces, suffer from a structural lag in education, access to drinking water and sanitation infrastructure. Conversely, large cities such as Johannesburg and Cape Town concentrate wealth and opportunity.

Health and education: the pillars of fragile development

On health, South Africa has made notable progress in the fight against HIV/AIDS. The prevalence rate, once above 20%, is now estimated at 13% thanks to a free, large-scale antiretroviral treatment policy. Average life expectancy, meanwhile, has risen to 65 years, from 52 years in the early 2000s.

In education, the literacy rate now stands at 94%, and higher education is attracting a growing number of African students. However, the poor quality of public schooling and the brain drain abroad continue to limit the benefits of these advances.

Towards more inclusive development

The South African government has launched several initiatives to promote inclusive growth, notably the "Vision 2030" plan, inspired by the National Development Plan. This plan aims to reduce poverty to below 10%, raise life expectancy to 70 years and create millions of sustainable jobs through the energy transition and new technologies.

But the success of this ambition will depend on fighting corruption, strengthening democratic institutions and achieving a better redistribution of wealth.

South Africa remains an unavoidable African power, with considerable economic and human potential. However, its development is still held back by deep inequalities and social divides inherited from apartheid. The improvement in its Human Development Index, though encouraging, will be sustainable only if it establishes equitable growth centred on people, education and social justice.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
